GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__Comprehensive Geri:
Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is a multidimensional, multidisciplinary diagnostic and management process for frail older people. It is NOT a single test or score: a coordinated team systematically evaluates four domains — medical, functional, psychological and social/environmental — and produces a problem list plus an individualised, coordinated care plan with structured follow-up. Robust trial evidence shows CGA increases the likelihood of a patient being alive and living in their own home at follow-up and reduces institutionalisation.

1INDICATION — who benefits and why

CGA is targeted at frail older adults with complexity, not simply anyone over a certain age. The principle is that in frailty, disease presents atypically and problems are interdependent (the “geriatric giants”: immobility, instability/falls, incontinence, impaired cognition, iatrogenesis). A single-organ, single-clinician approach misses interacting problems, so a structured multidomain review uncovers reversible contributors that a standard clerking overlooks.

Best evidence is for inpatient CGA on a dedicated geriatric ward and for older people admitted with an acute illness or after a fall.
Frailty screening (e.g. Clinical Frailty Scale, gait speed, PRISMA-7) helps select who should receive full CGA.
Also delivered in the community, care homes, surgical liaison (peri-operative “POPS”) and oncology.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the four domains and the team

Each core member assesses their domain, findings are pooled at a multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting, a shared problem list is drawn up, goals are agreed with the patient, interventions are actioned and reviewed. It is a cyclical process: assess → plan → intervene → reassess.

🩺Medical
Comorbidity, medication review/deprescribing, nutrition, continence, pain
🚶Functional
ADLs & IADLs, mobility, balance, falls risk, gait
🧠Psychological
Cognition (delirium/dementia), mood/depression, capacity
🏠Social / environmental
Support network, care package, finances/benefits, housing, carer strain
Geriatrician — medical diagnosis, medication optimisation, overall coordination.
Nurse — continence, skin/pressure areas, day-to-day function, delirium screening.
Physiotherapist (PT) — mobility, balance, falls and strength.
Occupational therapist (OT) — ADLs, home hazards, equipment, discharge assessment.
SALT — swallow (aspiration risk) and communication.
Pharmacist — polypharmacy review, deprescribing (STOPP/START).
Social worker — care package, safeguarding, placement, finances.
± dietitian, psychiatry/psychology, podiatry as needed.
3INTERPRETATION — turning findings into a plan

There is no numeric CGA cut-off; the “output” is a synthesised problem list and directed actions. Domain tools each carry their own thresholds that feed the plan.

Barthel Index low / declining→Significant ADL dependence → PT/OT rehab goals, care package
4AT ≥ 4→Delirium likely → screen for and treat precipitants
Clinical Frailty Scale 5–8→Mild–to–severe frailty → prioritise full CGA and ceiling-of-care/ReSPECT discussion
MUST ≥ 2→High malnutrition risk → dietitian referral, nutritional support
Multiple falls / gait instability→Multifactorial falls assessment, medication review, bone health
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Benefit depends on coordination and follow-up — a one-off assessment with no actioned plan or review loses the mortality/independence benefit.
Resource-intensive; must be targeted at frailty, not applied indiscriminately to all older inpatients.
Patient goals and capacity must be central — avoid paternalistic plans; involve family/advocates appropriately.
Do not miss delirium masquerading as dementia; cognition should be reassessed once acutely well.
🚩 CGA must actively screen for delirium and its precipitants (infection, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, pain, drugs). Anchoring on a “frail confused” label and mislabelling reversible delirium as fixed dementia leads to missed sepsis, inappropriate placement and avoidable death.
🎓 High-yield: CGA is a process, not a score. In trials it increases the chance of being alive and in one’s own home and reduces care-home admission — strongest evidence for inpatients on a dedicated geriatric ward. Remember the four domains (medical, functional, psychological, social) and that the deliverable is a coordinated problem list with follow-up.
Where CGA is delivered→best evidence on a dedicated geriatric ward, but increasingly at the front door (ED / acute frailty unit / frailty SDEC) to enable early assessment and avoid admission/deconditioning; also orthogeriatric hip-fracture co-management, perioperative POPS, community and care homes, with review via virtual ward / hospital-at-home.
Evidence & scope→Cochrane: CGA increases the likelihood of being alive and in one’s own home and reduces institutionalisation (NNT ~13). Four core domains (some models add a fifth spiritual/existential domain near end of life).
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__Clinical Frailty S:
The Clinical Frailty Scale (Rockwood CFS) is a 9-point, judgement-based ordinal scale that summarises a person's overall fitness or frailty on the 2 weeks before an acute illness. It is not a questionnaire and has no arithmetic score — the clinician synthesises mobility, function, cognition and comorbidity into a single grade from 1 (Very Fit) to 9 (Terminally Ill). The electronic Frailty Index (eFI) is a complementary deficit-accumulation tool built automatically from primary-care coded records (~36 deficits) that categorises a patient as fit, mild, moderate or severe frailty for population-level case-finding.

1INDICATION — why frailty grading matters

Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve where a minor stressor (infection, new drug, surgery) triggers a disproportionate decline. Grading it gives a rapid, reproducible prognostic marker that outperforms age alone.

Higher CFS predicts mortality, prolonged length of stay, delirium, falls, institutionalisation and readmission.
Used to shape shared decisions on escalation, critical-care admission, surgery, treatment intensity and anticipatory/advance care planning (e.g. ReSPECT).
eFI is used proactively in primary care to case-find and target Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment, medication review and falls services.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

CFS: Take a collateral/functional history anchored to the fortnight before the presenting illness. Judge mobility, help needed with instrumental ADLs (shopping, finances, medications) and personal ADLs (dressing, bathing, toileting), and cognition, then assign the single best-fit level. It takes under a minute at the bedside and is validated in adults ≥65.

eFI: Runs automatically over the GP record, counting the presence of coded deficits (symptoms, signs, diseases, disabilities) out of ~36. The index = deficits present ÷ deficits measured, generating a continuous 0–1 score mapped to bands.

🚩 The CFS is not validated in younger adults, in stable long-standing single-system disability (e.g. lifelong cerebral palsy or a stable spinal-cord injury), or in learning disability — scoring these groups can wrongly label them as frail. Grade the baseline, never the acute deterioration in front of you.
3INTERPRETATION — the bands
🟢1 Very Fit
Robust, active, exercise regularly, among fittest for age
🟢2 Fit
No active disease symptoms, active occasionally/seasonally
🟢3 Managing Well
Medical problems well controlled, not regularly active beyond walking
🟡4 Very Mild Frailty
Vulnerable; not dependent but symptoms limit activity, “slowed up”
🟡5 Mildly Frail
Needs help with instrumental ADLs (finances, transport, heavy chores, meds)
🟠6 Moderately Frail
Needs help with all outside activities and bathing; some help dressing
🔴7 Severely Frail
Completely dependent for personal care; stable, not high risk of dying
🔴8 Very Severely Frail
Completely dependent, approaching end of life; could not recover from minor illness
⚫9 Terminally Ill
Life expectancy <6 months, not otherwise evidently frail
CFS 1–3→Fit / not frail — manage as physiologically robust
CFS 4→Vulnerable / pre-frail — the tipping point; prompts closer review
CFS 5–6→Mild–moderate frailty — trigger Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment
CFS 7–9→Severe frailty / end of life — prioritise ceilings of care and advance care planning
eFI ≤0.12→Fit
eFI >0.12–0.24→Mild frailty
eFI >0.24–0.36→Moderate frailty
eFI >0.36→Severe frailty
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Baseline, not the crisis: a septic patient who was independent a fortnight ago is not CFS 7 today — capture the pre-morbid state.
Never a rationing tool in isolation: NICE and the British Geriatrics Society are explicit that a single CFS number must not be used to deny treatment, ITU or CPR; it informs, not decides.
Judgement dependent: inter-rater variability rises without training; anchor descriptors reduce drift.
eFI limitations: only as good as GP coding — missing codes underestimate frailty, and it lags real-time clinical change.
🚩 Using CFS alone to withhold escalation is unsafe and, during COVID-19, prompted a formal NICE clarification: frailty scores must be combined with the whole clinical picture, comorbidities and the patient's own wishes. Cognitive impairment/dementia is graded within CFS itself (usually 5–7 depending on dependency), not scored separately.
🎓 High-yield: CFS reflects the 2 weeks before the acute illness, is validated in adults ≥65, and CFS ≥5 is the common threshold to trigger Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment and a frailty pathway. It is judgement-based (no adding up), whereas the eFI is a counted deficit-accumulation index from primary-care data.
The two models of frailty→Cumulative-deficit model (Rockwood CFS / eFI — count/judge accumulated deficits) vs the Fried phenotype (unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weak grip, slow gait, low activity — ≥3 of 5 = frail, 1–2 = pre-frail, 0 = robust).
Using the score→CFS ≥5 flags frailty and triggers a CGA / frailty pathway; the number informs but must never alone decide escalation, ITU admission or CPR.
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__4AT (Delirium Scre:
The 4AT is a rapid, four-item bedside screening tool for delirium (and to a lesser extent cognitive impairment) in adults, designed for routine use in emergency departments, acute medical and surgical wards, and geriatric settings. It takes under 2 minutes, requires no special training, and crucially can be completed even in drowsy or uncooperative patients who cannot manage longer cognitive tests. A score of ≥4 flags possible delirium and should trigger a full diagnostic workup.

1INDICATION — why the 4AT exists

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness precipitated by an underlying medical cause. It affects up to a fifth of general hospital inpatients and a higher proportion of older and post-operative patients, yet it is missed in more than half of cases when no structured screen is used, particularly the hypoactive (quiet, withdrawn) subtype.

Delirium independently predicts prolonged admission, falls, new institutionalisation, persistent cognitive decline and increased mortality, so early detection matters. The 4AT was built for real-world case-finding: unlike the CAM it needs no formal training, and unlike the MMSE or MoCA it does not require the patient to write, draw or fully cooperate.

Use it: on admission of older or frail patients, after surgery, and whenever acute confusion or behavioural change is suspected.
Strength: valid in the arousable-but-drowsy patient — abnormal alertness itself scores positive rather than making the test impossible.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the four items

Score the four items in order; no equipment is needed. Observe the patient, then ask the four AMT questions, then the attention task, then establish acute change from a collateral history or notes.

👁️1. Alertness
Observe (rouse briefly if asleep). Normal or mildly sleepy for <10s after waking = 0; clearly abnormal (drowsy, agitated, hard to rouse) = 4.
🧠2. AMT4
Age, date of birth, place (name of hospital/building), current year. 0 errors = 0; 1 error = 1; ≥2 errors = 2.
📅3. Attention
Months of the year backwards from December. ≥7 correct = 0; <7 or refuses = 1; untestable (drowsy/inattentive) = 2.
🔄4. Acute change / fluctuation
Evidence of acute change or fluctuating course in alertness, cognition or mental function (last 2 weeks, still evident in last 24h). No = 0; Yes = 4.

Sum the four items for a total of 0–12.

3INTERPRETATION — the score bands
≥4→Possible delirium ± cognitive impairment — do a full delirium assessment
1–3→Possible cognitive impairment — consider further cognitive testing and collateral history
0→Delirium or severe cognitive impairment unlikely (delirium still possible if items 1 or 4 incomplete)

Note the built-in weighting: an abnormal alertness score (4) or a positive acute-change item (4) each pushes the total straight to the ≥4 delirium band on its own, reflecting how central impaired arousal and acute fluctuation are to the diagnosis.

A positive 4AT (≥4) should prompt a structured cause search — the PINCH ME mnemonic: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment.
The TIME bundle (Think exclude/Investigate/Manage/Engage) structures the response once delirium is flagged.
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
It is a screen, not a diagnosis. A positive result requires clinical confirmation of delirium (e.g. against DSM-5 criteria); a negative result does not exclude it, especially if alertness or acute-change data are missing.
It cannot distinguish delirium from dementia by itself. A high score in a patient with known dementia may reflect baseline impairment — item 4 (acute change from baseline) and collateral history are what separate the two.
Language and sensory barriers (deafness, dysphasia, no shared language) reduce reliability; document these.
Repeat it. Delirium fluctuates, so a single negative screen in a high-risk patient warrants re-testing.
🚩 A positive 4AT is not the endpoint — it is a prompt to find the cause. Delirium is a medical emergency: hypoactive delirium in particular is easily dismissed as tiredness or depression, yet may signal sepsis, hypoxia, urinary retention, hypoglycaemia or an adverse drug effect. Never label acute confusion as "just their dementia" or sedate an agitated patient before excluding a reversible precipitant.
🎓 Two items carry a weight of 4: abnormal alertness and acute change/fluctuation. Either one alone gives a score of 4 and places the patient in the possible-delirium band — a favourite exam point, because it shows the tool is deliberately biased towards catching the drowsy, fluctuating patient that longer tests would miss.
Once the 4AT is positive — manage→treat the precipitant; first-line is non-pharmacological (reorientation, glasses/hearing aids, familiar faces, day–night lighting, hydration, mobilise, minimise ward moves/lines) and review/stop deliriogenic drugs. Delirium ›
Agitated delirium needing sedation→only if severe distress or risk → short-term low-dose haloperidol; AVOID antipsychotics in Parkinson’s / Lewy body dementia → use lorazepam. Parkinson’s ›
Precipitant work-up (PINCH ME)→obs/NEWS, capillary glucose, bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP, Ca, LFT, TFT, B12), urinalysis + culture, bladder scan (retention), sats/ABG (hypoxia), ECG, medication review; CT head/EEG only if focal signs or no cause found.
Motor subtypes / the 3 Ds→hyperactive, hypoactive (commonest, most missed, worst prognosis) or mixed. Contrast: delirium (acute, fluctuating, inattention, altered consciousness) vs dementia (chronic, progressive) vs depression (low mood/anhedonia, subacute). Dementias ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Positive 4AT → find & treat the cause + non-pharmacological measures first. Sedation only if severe distress: haloperidol, EXCEPT Parkinson’s/Lewy body → lorazepam. Hypoactive delirium is the commonest and most missed.
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__Timed Up-and-Go &:
The Timed Up-and-Go (TUG) is a quick, validated bedside test of functional mobility, balance and lower-limb strength used to screen older adults for falls risk. The patient rises from a standard armchair without pushing off with the arms, walks 3 metres, turns, walks back and sits down; the time taken (seconds) plus the quality of movement is recorded. It is one component of a wider multifactorial falls assessment, not a stand-alone diagnostic test.

1INDICATION – when and why

Used to screen community-dwelling and hospitalised older adults for impaired mobility and falls risk, and to trigger a fuller assessment. NICE recommends asking all people aged ≥65 about falls; those reporting a fall or gait/balance problems should have their mobility observed – the TUG is a practical way to do this.

Integrates strength (standing from a chair), gait, dynamic balance and the ability to turn safely into a single timed task.
Useful for tracking change over time (e.g. before and after a strength-and-balance programme).
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED – the protocol

Standardise the set-up so results are comparable and repeatable.

Use a standard armchair (seat height ~46 cm, with armrests) placed against a wall; mark a line on the floor at exactly 3 metres.
Patient wears usual footwear and may use their usual walking aid (record which aid is used).
On the word “go”, the patient stands without using the arms if able, walks to the line at a comfortable, safe pace, turns, returns and sits down.
Time from “go” until the buttocks touch the seat again. One practice trial is allowed; a walking aid is permitted but noted.
3INTERPRETATION – time and quality

Record both the seconds and the observed movement quality – a “normal” time with poor technique is still concerning.

<10 seconds→Normal functional mobility in a healthy adult
≥12 seconds→Increased falls risk – warrants further multifactorial assessment
≥14 seconds→Commonly quoted higher-risk threshold predicting future falls
Unsteadiness, staggering turn, hesitancy, using arms to rise→Qualitatively abnormal – refer regardless of the raw time
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & ACTION

The TUG is a screen, not a diagnosis: a slow or unsafe result should prompt a broader, cause-directed work-up.

Cut-offs vary with age, comorbidity and setting – a single value should not be used in isolation.
A slow/unsafe TUG → refer for strength-and-balance training (physiotherapy / falls clinic), review culprit medications (sedatives, antihypertensives, anticholinergics), check vision and postural blood pressure, and treat contributing causes.
Confounded by pain, acute illness, arthritis, footwear and language/cognitive barriers.
🪑Chair rise
Lower-limb (quadriceps) strength – arms used = weakness
🚶Gait
Speed, stride, symmetry, festination or shuffling
🔄180° turn
Dynamic balance – multi-step or staggering turn is high-risk
🦯Aid use
Stick/frame reliance signals reduced independence
🚩 Never leave the patient unattended: a frail person can fall during the test itself. Stay within arm’s reach, guard on the turn (the highest-risk phase), and do not proceed if the patient is acutely unwell, has unexplained syncope, or is clearly too unsafe to attempt standing.
🎓 High-yield: quote ≥12 seconds as the screening threshold for increased falls risk (≥14s often cited for predicting falls), and remember the TUG is scored for BOTH time and quality – observing an unsteady turn or reliance on the armrests is as important as the stopwatch.
Gait pattern → lesion
  • Antalgic (short stance on painful side) = pain / OA. Trendelenburg / waddling = hip-abductor weakness or proximal myopathy.
  • Cerebellar ataxic = broad-based, veering. Sensory ataxic = stamping, Romberg-positive (dorsal column/proprioceptive loss).
  • Parkinsonian = shuffling/festinant, reduced arm swing, en-bloc turn. High-steppage / foot drop = common peroneal / L5. Spastic / scissoring = UMN/cord. Magnetic / apraxic = NPH/frontal.
Pattern-specific next steps→Parkinsonian → neurology ± DaT scan. Foot drop → nerve conduction studies/EMG. Magnetic gait + urinary incontinence + cognitive decline (“wet, wacky, wobbly”) → CT/MRI head + tap test = NPH. Spastic → cord imaging. NPH/Hydrocephalus › Parkinson’s ›
Quantitative gait speed→<0.8 m/s = adverse marker of falls, frailty and mortality (roughly 1.0 m/s is needed to cross a road safely).
🎓 Exam pearl. Romberg-positive = sensory (not cerebellar) ataxia. Magnetic gait + incontinence + cognitive decline = NPH (CT/MRI + tap test). Gait speed <0.8 m/s is an adverse marker.
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__Barthel Index (Fun:
The Barthel Index is a validated ordinal scale that quantifies a patient's functional independence across 10 basic activities of daily living (ADLs). It does not diagnose disease; it measures what the patient can actually do, generating a number used to plan discharge, target rehabilitation, size a care package, and track functional trajectory over time. Higher scores mean greater independence.

1INDICATION — when and why it is used

Core tool of comprehensive geriatric assessment, stroke rehabilitation and discharge planning. It answers the practical question “how much help does this person need?” The principle is function, not pathology: two patients with the same diagnosis may have very different Barthel scores, and it is the score — not the diagnosis — that predicts care needs.

Baseline on admission, then serial scoring to demonstrate rehabilitation progress or decline.
Informs multidisciplinary team decisions on discharge destination (home, home-with-package, or bedded rehab/residential care).
Outcome measure in stroke and rehabilitation research.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the 10 domains and scoring

Score each of 10 ADLs by observed or reliably reported current performance (what the patient does, not what they theoretically could do). Most domains score 0, 5 or 10, but bathing and grooming score 0–5 and transfers and mobility 0–15; the total is summed to 0–100 in 5-point steps (an older version scores 0–20). Use of aids while remaining independent still scores full marks.

🍽️Feeding
Cutting, spreading, getting food to mouth
🛁Bathing
All-or-nothing: independent (5) or not (0)
🪥Grooming
Face, hair, teeth, shaving
👕Dressing
Including buttons, zips, laces
💩Bowels
Continence over preceding week
💧Bladder
Continence; ability to manage catheter
🚽Toilet use
Transfers on/off, clothing, wiping
🛏️Transfers
Bed to chair (0–15, graded by helpers)
🚶Mobility
On level (0–15); wheelchair scores partial
🪜Stairs
Independent, with help, or unable

Note the two mobility-related domains (transfers and mobility) carry a maximum of 15 each, which is why they dominate the total.

3INTERPRETATION — reading the score and its trajectory

There is no single validated cut-off; the score is best read as a gradient of dependency and, above all, as a trajectory on serial measurement. Commonly examined bands:

100 / 100→Fully independent in basic ADLs (does NOT mean able to live alone — iADLs untested)
≥ 60→Broadly independent / minimal assistance; often compatible with discharge home
40–55→Moderate dependency — needs a package of care or rehabilitation
< 40→Severe dependency — substantial or 24-hour support required
0 / 100→Totally dependent / bedbound
Falling serial score→Functional decline — actively search for reversible causes and re-scale support
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Ceiling effect: a fit but frail person can score 100 yet still be unable to shop, cook or manage finances — the index misses instrumental ADLs.
Floor effect: two profoundly dependent patients both score 0 despite differing needs, so change becomes hard to detect at the extreme.
Does not measure cognition, mood or safety awareness — a wandering patient with dementia may score highly.
Insensitive to small but meaningful changes because of the 5-point granularity.
Vulnerable to reporter bias if scored on what the patient could do rather than actual performance.
🚩 A high or “normal” Barthel score does NOT confirm a patient is safe to live alone or be discharged. Because it ignores cognition, iADLs and safety awareness, relying on it in isolation can send a patient with dementia or an unsafe home environment back to harm. Always combine it with a cognitive assessment, an iADL/social assessment and multidisciplinary judgement.
🎓 High-yield: the Barthel Index covers basic ADLs only (feeding, bathing, grooming, dressing, bowels, bladder, toilet, transfers, mobility, stairs). If a question mentions cooking, shopping, managing money or medications, or using the telephone, those are instrumental ADLs and fall OUTSIDE the Barthel — a classic exam trap.
Barthel low or falling — what to do→refer to OT/PT for a rehabilitation programme, provide equipment and home adaptations (grab rails, raised toilet seat, perching stool, commode) and size the care package to the score, while searching for reversible causes (delirium, infection, pain, polypharmacy, malnutrition). Delirium › Falls ›
Basic ADLs fine but is it safe to live alone?→assess instrumental ADLs with the Lawton IADL scale — telephone, shopping, food preparation, housekeeping, laundry, transport, responsibility for medications and handling finances.
🎓 Exam pearl. The Barthel measures basic ADLs; pair it with the Lawton IADL scale for instrumental ADLs and a cognitive assessment before judging whether someone can live alone. A low or falling score triggers OT/PT rehab, equipment/adaptations and a hunt for reversible causes.
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__STOPP/START & Anti:
STOPP/START are the two halves of an evidence-based, explicit medication-review tool for older adults, applied alongside an Anticholinergic Burden (ACB) score during a structured medication review in polypharmacy. STOPP (Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions) flags potentially inappropriate medications that should be stopped; START (Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment) flags evidence-based treatments that have been wrongly omitted. Together they address both over-prescribing and under-prescribing, while ACB quantifies the cumulative sedative-anticholinergic load that drives falls, delirium and cognitive decline.

1INDICATION — who is reviewed and why

Applied to patients typically ≥65 years on multiple medications (polypharmacy commonly defined as ≥5 regular drugs; problematic polypharmacy where harm outweighs benefit). The principle is that ageing alters pharmacokinetics (reduced renal clearance, lower lean body mass, increased fat distribution) and pharmacodynamics (greater CNS sensitivity), so drugs safe in younger adults accumulate and cause harm. A structured review is triggered by falls, delirium/cognitive decline, a new prescribing cascade, admission, or a care-home medication review.

STOPP identifies potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) to deprescribe.
START identifies potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) to add.
ACB scores the cumulative anticholinergic exposure across the whole regimen.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the review protocol

Compile a complete, reconciled drug list (including over-the-counter and herbal agents), the indication for each drug, renal/hepatic function and current problems. Screen the list against the STOPP criteria (drugs to stop) and the START criteria (treatments to start), then total the ACB by summing the score of every anticholinergic agent. Decisions are shared with the patient, and stopping is usually staged with planned tapering and monitoring rather than abrupt cessation of all agents at once.

🛑STOPP example
Long-term benzodiazepine — falls & sedation risk
🛑STOPP example
NSAID with eGFR <50 — AKI risk
✅START example
Anticoagulation in AF — stroke prevention
✅START example
Bone protection with long-term steroid
🧠ACB agent
Amitriptyline, oxybutynin = 3 points each
🧠ACB agent
Codeine, furosemide = 1 point each
3INTERPRETATION — thresholds and actions
Any STOPP criterion met→Potentially inappropriate medication — review for deprescribing
Any START criterion met→Evidence-based omission — consider starting the treatment
ACB total 1–2→Lower burden — minimise where feasible
ACB total ≥3→High burden — associated with falls, cognitive impairment, delirium and increased mortality; actively deprescribe
Each +1 rise in ACB→Incremental increase in cognitive decline and fall risk
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
The tools are explicit criteria — they support but do not replace individualised clinical judgement and patient goals.
A flag is a prompt to review, not an automatic instruction to stop or start; benefit versus harm must still be weighed.
Abruptly stopping several drugs at once risks withdrawal (benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, SSRIs) and destabilisation — taper and monitor.
ACB scales are not identical; the same drug may score differently on different lists, and low-scoring drugs still add up.
Deprescribing needs follow-up to confirm the change was safe and to catch return of the original indication.
🚩 Never stop long-term benzodiazepines, opioids, beta-blockers or SSRIs abruptly in an older patient — sudden cessation can precipitate seizures, rebound hypertension/angina or a withdrawal syndrome. Reduce in staged steps with monitoring.
🎓 Remember the split: STOPP = stop the wrong drugs (over-prescribing), START = start the missing drugs (under-prescribing). An ACB of ≥3 is the exam-favourite high-burden threshold linked to falls, delirium and mortality.
5KEY PRESCRIBING-SAFETY CONCEPTS
  • Prescribing cascade — a drug’s side effect is misread as a new disease and treated with a second drug (e.g. amlodipine → ankle oedema → furosemide; metoclopramide → drug-induced parkinsonism → levodopa). The fix is to stop drug 1, not add drug 2.
  • FRIDs (falls-risk-increasing drugs) — systematically review benzodiazepines/Z-drugs and other sedatives, antihypertensives/nitrates/alpha-blockers (orthostasis), anticholinergics, opioids and antipsychotics in any faller; check lying/standing BP and deprescribe.
  • Polypharmacy harms — adverse drug reactions, drug–drug and drug–disease interactions, prescribing cascades, falls, non-adherence, pill burden and hospital admissions.
  • Anticholinergic syndrome — peripheral (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision) plus central confusion/delirium: “mad, dry, red, hot, blind”. Other ACB-3 agents: chlorphenamine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, tolterodine/solifenacin, TCAs.
  • Beers criteria = US explicit list of potentially inappropriate medications only; STOPP/START (European) adds the START omissions half, so it also flags under-prescribing.
After a fall or new delirium, screen the drug chart→identify FRIDs and high-ACB drugs and deprescribe, and recognise any prescribing cascade. Falls › Delirium › Polypharmacy ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Spot the prescribing cascade: a new symptom soon after starting a drug is an ADR until proven otherwise — review/stop the culprit rather than adding another drug. Beers = US PIM list; STOPP/START also covers under-prescribing.
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__ADRT / DNACPR / Re:
Advance care planning (ACP) lets a person shape the care they would want if they lose capacity in the future. In England & Wales three instruments dominate: an ADRT (a legally binding refusal of specified treatment made while the person has capacity), a DNACPR (a clinical decision that CPR will not be attempted), and ReSPECT (a summary emergency plan of recommendations). All operate within the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA), whose five principles — presumption of capacity; all practicable support to help someone decide; an unwise decision is not itself incapacity; best interests; and least-restrictive intervention — underpin every step.

1INDICATION — why these frameworks exist

People with progressive, life-limiting or high-relapse conditions may lose capacity acutely (delirium, arrest, terminal decline). ACP records their wishes in advance so that emergency decisions honour autonomy rather than default to maximal intervention. The legal engine is the MCA 2005: a person may refuse future treatment while capacitous, and clinicians must otherwise act in a patient's best interests.

📜ADRT
Patient's own binding REFUSAL of a specified treatment; a decision, not a recommendation
🫀DNACPR
Clinical decision that CPR will not be attempted; applies to CPR only
📋ReSPECT
Summary emergency plan of RECOMMENDATIONS incl. CPR status; not legally binding
👤LPA (H&W)
Appointed PROXY who decides for the person once they lack capacity
2HOW THEY ARE MADE — validity requirements

Each instrument has distinct formalities. An ADRT refusing life-sustaining treatment carries the strictest requirements.

ADRT: made by an adult (≥18) with capacity; must specify the treatment refused and the circumstances. If it refuses life-sustaining treatment it must be written, signed and witnessed and explicitly state it applies ‘even if life is at risk’.
DNACPR: a clinical decision signed by a senior clinician. Patient consent is not required, but there is a legal duty to consult and inform the patient (or, if they lack capacity, those close to them — per Tracey and Winspear).
ReSPECT: completed through conversation with the patient (or proxy/family); records clinical recommendations including a CPR decision. It is a plan, signed by a clinician, that travels with the patient across settings.
LPA (health & welfare): registered with the Office of the Public Guardian; the attorney may refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA expressly grants that power.
3INTERPRETATION — what applies when
Valid + applicable ADRT refusing this treatment→Legally BINDING — must be followed; overriding it may be battery
ADRT that is invalid or not applicable to the situation→Not binding; decide in best interests (ADRT still informs the view)
DNACPR in place→Do NOT attempt CPR; ALL other treatment (oxygen, antibiotics, fluids) continues as indicated
ReSPECT form recommendation→Guides the responding team but is NOT legally binding on its own
Registered LPA (H&W) with life-sustaining power vs an ADRT→The one made LATER prevails (a later valid LPA can override an earlier ADRT, and vice versa)
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
An ADRT cannot demand a treatment, cannot refuse basic care (warmth, hygiene, oral food/fluids), and cannot refuse treatment for a mental disorder if the person is detained under the Mental Health Act.
A DNACPR is not a ceiling of care and never means ‘do not treat’ — escalation, ITU or active treatment can still be appropriate.
Capacity is decision- and time-specific: a person may lack capacity for finances yet retain it for an ADRT, and vice versa.
Documents must be located and checked in an emergency; verbal ADRTs are valid for non-life-sustaining treatment but hard to evidence.
🚩 Never assume a DNACPR removes other active treatment, and never treat a ReSPECT recommendation as consent to withhold care without confirming the patient's wishes. Conversely, an emergency team that resuscitates a patient against a valid and applicable ADRT commits an unlawful act — always look for and honour a valid ADRT before initiating life-sustaining treatment.
🎓 High-yield distinction: an ADRT refuses treatment (the patient decides in advance), whereas an LPA for health & welfare appoints a proxy to decide later. Only a written, signed and witnessed ADRT stating it applies ‘even if life is at risk’ can refuse life-sustaining treatment.
Advance statement (wishes, values, preferences)→not legally binding, but must be considered in a best-interests decision — contrast the binding ADRT, which refuses a specified treatment.
Emergency / arrest, wishes unknown→look for a valid & applicable ADRT / ReSPECT / DNACPR; honour a valid ADRT; if none is found and the patient lacks capacity, treat in their best interests — do not delay CPR to hunt for paperwork.
ReSPECT is more than a DNACPR→clinician-completed through shared decision-making; it records what care the person would want (e.g. hospital admission, escalation) as well as ceilings/DNACPR — recommendations, not consent or a binding order.
A DNACPR is not permanent→it is reviewable and can be revoked if the clinical situation or the patient’s wishes change.
No LPA in place?→the Court of Protection may appoint a health-and-welfare deputy, but a deputy cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment (unlike an expressly authorised LPA).
🎓 Exam pearl. Binding vs advisory is the classic trap: ADRT (valid & applicable) and an LPA’s authorised decision are binding; an advance statement and a ReSPECT form are not (considered, not obeyed). A DNACPR is a clinical CPR-only decision — no consent needed, but a duty to consult.
GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT__DoLS / Deprivation:
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) are a statutory framework under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 that lawfully authorise the deprivation of liberty of a person aged ≥18 who lacks capacity to consent to their care or accommodation arrangements, where those arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty in a hospital or care home and are necessary and in the person's best interests. DoLS exist to protect the individual's Article 5 right to liberty by providing independent assessment, time-limited authorisation, review and a right of appeal to the Court of Protection.

1INDICATION — WHEN DoLS APPLIES & THE 'ACID TEST'

DoLS is triggered when a person who lacks capacity to consent to their residence/care is being deprived of their liberty. The threshold comes from the Supreme Court in Cheshire West (2014), known as the acid test:

The person is under continuous supervision and control, AND
The person is not free to leave the place where they live.

Crucially, the person's compliance or lack of objection is irrelevant, and the reason/purpose (however benign) and normality of the placement do not matter — a deprivation is a deprivation. Typical examples: a patient with advanced dementia on a locked ward, kept under 1:1 observation and returned if they try to leave.

2HOW IT IS AUTHORISED — THE PROCESS

The care home or hospital (the managing authority) applies to the supervisory body (the local authority) for a standard authorisation. Where a deprivation must begin immediately, the managing authority can grant itself an urgent authorisation lasting up to 7 days (extendable to 14) while the standard assessment is completed.

The supervisory body arranges six qualifying assessments, completed by at least two independent assessors (a doctor — the Mental Health Assessor — and a Best Interests Assessor):

🎂Age
Person is aged 18 or over.
🧠Mental Health
Has a mental disorder (as defined by the MHA 1983).
⚖️Mental Capacity
Lacks capacity to decide about their accommodation for care/treatment.
❤️Best Interests
Deprivation is occurring, and is necessary & proportionate to risk of harm.
🔀Eligibility
Not otherwise ineligible — e.g. not detained/conflicting with the MHA.
📝No Refusals
No conflict with a valid advance decision or a decision by a donee/deputy.

If all six are met, a standard authorisation is granted for a maximum of 12 months. A Relevant Person's Representative (RPR) and access to an IMCA support the person and their right to challenge.

3INTERPRETATION & KEY THRESHOLDS
Acid test both limbs met + lacks capacity→Deprivation of liberty — DoLS authorisation required
Urgent authorisation→Managing authority self-grants; lasts up to 7 days (extendable to 14)
Standard authorisation→Granted by supervisory body; maximum duration 12 months
Setting is the person's OWN HOME / supported living→DoLS does NOT apply — authorise via Court of Protection instead
Person / RPR wishes to challenge→Appeal to the Court of Protection under s21A MCA
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & DoLS vs MHA

DoLS applies only in hospitals and care homes — it cannot authorise deprivation in a person's own home, supported living or other community settings, which require a Court of Protection order. It authorises the deprivation of liberty itself, not specific treatment; treatment decisions still rest on best-interests principles under the wider MCA.

DoLS vs the Mental Health Act 1983: use the MHA when the primary purpose is to detain and treat a mental disorder and the person objects to that admission/treatment; use DoLS/MCA when the person lacks capacity, is compliant/not objecting, and the deprivation relates to care generally (often physical-health or dementia care). A patient who lacks capacity and objects to psychiatric admission is ineligible for DoLS and should be assessed under the MHA.

DoLS is widely criticised as bureaucratic and is legislated to be replaced by the Liberty Protection Safeguards (LPS) (implementation paused in 2023, so DoLS remains in force), which extend cover to 16–17 year olds and to all settings including the community.

🚩 A person who lacks capacity but is actively objecting to admission or treatment for a mental disorder is generally ineligible for DoLS — do not use DoLS to bypass the Mental Health Act. Using the wrong framework leaves the deprivation unlawful and breaches Article 5. Equally, never rely on a patient's passive compliance to avoid seeking authorisation.
🎓 The Cheshire West acid test has just two limbs: continuous supervision and control AND not free to leave. Remember Baroness Hale's phrase — “a gilded cage is still a cage” — the person's contentment, the good intentions of carers, and the comfort of the placement are all irrelevant to whether a deprivation exists.
Ward doctor spots a patient without capacity stopped from leaving→in hospital the trust is the managing authority: it self-grants an urgent authorisation (lawful for up to 7 days) and applies to the local-authority supervisory body for a standard authorisation, documenting capacity and best interests meanwhile.
Who protects the person under a DoLS→a Relevant Person’s Representative (RPR) keeps contact and can trigger a challenge; an IMCA (Independent Mental Capacity Advocate, ss.39A/39D) provides independent advocacy and helps appeal to the Court of Protection (s21A).
🎓 Exam pearl. DoLS covers only hospitals and care homes; a deprivation in the person’s own home or supported living needs a Court of Protection order instead. In hospital, an urgent authorisation makes the deprivation lawful straight away while the standard authorisation is sought.
